title: Unless the Lord build (Psalm 126 [127])
hook: they labor in vain that build without him

segments.voice: Yesterday, I rejoiced: pilgrims inside Jerusalem's gates, praying for its peace. Your line was peace within thy walls. What did you do to make your walls more peaceful? Day one hundred eighty-six.

It's eleven at night. The laptop is still open. There's one more email, one more fix, one more thing, and you tell yourself if you just push a little longer, it'll all hold together. The coffee's cold. Tomorrow you'll get up early and do it again. It's the loop where everything seems to rest on one person, and stopping for a second feels like letting it all fall down. Long ago, someone wrote a psalm for exactly that person. Today: unless the Lord build.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, STILL WORKING.` → `IT ALL DEPENDS ON ME.` → `A PSALM FOR THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: Another of the gradual psalms, and the heading gives it to Solomon, the king who built the Temple. It opens with two pictures. In the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." First, notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say don't build. It doesn't say fire the watchman. The builder still lays bricks, and the guard still stands on the wall. The psalm is about who the work finally rests on. Second, the tired worker. The next verse says it's vain to rise before light, eating the bread of sorrow. And then comes a line of real gentleness. In the Douay-Rheims: "When he shall give sleep to his beloved." In the psalm, rest isn't laziness. It's trust: the house isn't held up by one pair of hands. Third, the house. In Hebrew, house can mean a building and also a family, a household, a line of children. So the psalm goes on to children as a gift from the Lord. Build a home, raise a family, run a city: the psalm says all of it rests on God first. The Latin opening, Nisi Dominus, was set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi, and it's carved as a motto over doors and on city arms. Catholics also have an old habit that fits it well: the morning offering, a prayer at the start of the day that hands over all the day's work before it begins.
screen: `TWO PICTURES: BUILDER AND WATCHMAN.` · `STILL BUILD. STILL WATCH.` · `SLEEP TO HIS BELOVED.` · `HOUSE MEANS FAMILY TOO.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer today's work before you start. Settle, and breathe. Name the main thing you'll work on today: a project, a shift, homework, looking after someone. See yourself starting it. Now, if you pray, hand it over: this is yours, Lord, before it's mine. Some Catholics use the morning offering for this. If you don't pray, simply set an intention: I'll do my part, and I won't carry the whole house alone. The bell holds the time.
Unless the Lord build. The first words of a psalm that says our work, our cities and our families rest on God, not on our effort alone. Today's word.
Your line: not in vain. Today, do your work well, and then, tonight, stop. Go to sleep without finishing everything. Day one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 126 [127] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some begin the day with a morning offering, a traditional prayer that offers the day's work, joys and sufferings to God.

original.note: Latin: unless the Lord, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate, set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning that hard work is pointless.
what it means: keep building and keeping watch, but the work rests on God, so you can also rest.
what a scholar hears: bayit, house, as building and household; a Solomon heading for the Temple builder's psalm.

notes: Douay-Rheims 126:1 given from memory; confirm. Douay 126:2 reads differently from the KJV ('when he shall give sleep to his beloved', from memory); the KJV line is quoted and named.
Heading 'A gradual canticle of Solomon': confirm the Douay heading.
Settings: Vivaldi (RV 608) and Monteverdi (Vespers of 1610) set Nisi Dominus. 'Nisi Dominus Frustra' is the motto of Edinburgh; the script mentions mottos on doors and city arms generally. Confirm.
'Three thousand years ago' in the hook: the psalm's date is uncertain; a Keeper may prefer 'long ago'.
The morning offering is described, not quoted or composed.
